course.title: The Rise of the Roman Empire
course.description: Follow Rome from a republic of elected magistrates to an empire governed from one city, and see what survived it.
course.audience: A general reader with no background in ancient history who wants an accurate outline supported by sources.

modules.title: From republic to empire
modules.description: Trace how Rome's shared republican authority gave way to rule by one man, and how that state was held together afterwards.

concepts.title: The Roman Republic
concepts.summary: The Republic governed Rome from 509 BCE through elected magistrates and a senate of former office-holders.

concepts.title: The crisis of the Republic
concepts.summary: Commanders who held long military commands and personal armies broke the Republic's habit of shared, temporary power.

concepts.title: Augustus and the principate
concepts.summary: Augustus kept the outward forms of the Republic while holding the legal powers that made him sole ruler.

concepts.title: Roman expansion
concepts.summary: War and annexation carried Roman rule around the Mediterranean and into western Europe over roughly four centuries.

concepts.title: Provinces and administration
concepts.summary: A province was governed by an appointed official who kept order and answered to Rome for the taxes it produced.

concepts.title: Roman roads
concepts.summary: Paved military roads let armies and official messages travel at a speed the state could plan around.

concepts.title: Roman citizenship
concepts.summary: Citizenship carried legal standing under Roman law and was extended to provincial populations over time.

concepts.title: Life in the Roman city
concepts.summary: Urban life centred on public buildings paid for by emperors and wealthy citizens, from bath houses to the amphitheatre.

concepts.title: The end of western rule and what followed
concepts.summary: Imperial rule ended in the west in 476 CE while the eastern half continued, and Roman law and Latin outlived both.

stageTitles.completion: The rise of the empire: done

blocks.text: Rome was a republic for nearly five centuries, then an empire for centuries more.
Before reading on, decide what you would expect to find at the boundary between the two. A decisive battle, perhaps, or something far less visible.
From 509 BCE, Roman citizens elected magistrates who held office for a fixed term, and a senate of former office-holders shaped policy.
The design of the Republic was that no single person kept power for long.
In the first century BCE commanders held long provincial commands and built armies loyal to themselves rather than to the state.
Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and started a civil war. His assassination in 44 BCE did not end it; Actium in 31 BCE did, leaving Octavian without a rival.
The order matters more than the dates. Put these four in sequence before naming the moment the Republic ended.
Given all that, pick the moment historians normally use.
In 27 BCE the Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus. Elections continued and the old offices were still filled, so a Roman of the day could say the Republic had been restored.

In practice Augustus held the powers that decided the army, the provinces, and who would follow him. That is the answer to the question you predicted: not a battle or a coronation, but a settlement that changed everything while announcing nothing.

blocks.text: At its height Rome governed tens of millions of people across three continents, using a few thousand Roman officials.
How? Commit to a guess before reading on.

Expansion took centuries and came in pieces. The wars with Carthage from 264 BCE brought Sicily, Spain and north Africa. Caesar took Gaul from 58 BCE. Claudius invaded Britain in 43 CE and Trajan annexed Dacia in 106 CE.
Conquered territory became a province under an appointed governor. He commanded the troops stationed there, heard legal cases, and answered to Rome for the taxes his province produced.
Local elites usually kept their positions and collected most of what Rome asked for.
That is the mechanism. Now name it.
Roads made the rest work. The Via Appia was begun in 312 BCE, and the network was built for the army: graded, paved, and usable in winter.
A governor's report could reach Rome on a known schedule, so a decision made in one city could be applied a thousand miles away.

stageTitles.review: Recall the city and the ending

blocks.text: 476 CE is the date usually given for the fall of Rome.
Before reading on, decide what you think actually stopped in that year, and what did not.
Roman city life ran on public building: bath houses, aqueducts, and places of entertainment, paid for by emperors and wealthy citizens who expected recognition in return.
The Colosseum was inaugurated in 80 CE and held tens of thousands of spectators at shows the state provided free.
Citizenship began as the status of the people of one city and was granted piecemeal to allies and veterans.
In 212 CE the Antonine Constitution extended it to almost every free inhabitant of the empire, placing a very large population under one body of law.
Now test the assumption in the date itself.
Constantine dedicated Constantinople in 330 CE. In 476 CE Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and no new emperor was appointed in the west.
Rule continued in the east for nearly another thousand years. Roman law, Latin, and the roads outlasted the western state entirely.

activities.title: From republic to empire
activities.instructions: Drag the year to reveal what had already happened by that date. Then answer the question below the track.

events.label: Traditional founding of Rome
events.detail: Later Roman writers dated the founding of their city to 753 BCE. The date is traditional rather than documented.

events.label: Republic established
events.detail: Rome expelled its last king and began electing magistrates who held office for a fixed term.

events.label: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
events.detail: Julius Caesar led an army out of his province into Italy, which began a civil war against the Senate's commanders.

events.label: Caesar assassinated
events.detail: Senators killed Caesar after he was made dictator for life. The killing restored no lasting republican government.

events.label: Battle of Actium
events.detail: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra, leaving Octavian without a rival for control of the Roman world.

events.label: Octavian becomes Augustus
events.detail: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus. He held the powers of sole ruler while the republican offices continued to be filled.

events.label: Greatest territorial extent
events.detail: At the death of Trajan the empire covered its largest area, reaching from Britain to Mesopotamia.

activities.title: The reach of Rome
activities.instructions: Drag the year to follow how far Roman control extended. Then answer the question below the track.

events.label: Via Appia begun
events.detail: The first great paved Roman road was started under the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, running south from Rome.

events.label: First Punic War begins
events.detail: The long conflict with Carthage began, and Rome built a fleet to fight it at sea.

events.label: Carthage destroyed
events.detail: Rome destroyed Carthage at the end of the Third Punic War and annexed its territory in north Africa.

events.label: Campaigns in Gaul begin
events.detail: Caesar's campaigns brought the whole of Gaul under Roman control within a decade.

events.label: Invasion of Britain
events.detail: Roman forces landed under the emperor Claudius and began the long annexation of southern Britain.

events.label: Dacia annexed
events.detail: Trajan's wars north of the Danube ended with Dacia becoming a Roman province.

events.label: Greatest territorial extent
events.detail: The empire reached its largest area at the death of Trajan, held together by roads and appointed governors.

questions.prompt: Which event marked the transition from the Roman Republic to rule by an emperor?
hints: Two of the options are earlier moments in the civil wars rather than the settlement that followed them.
Look for the moment when one man's position was formally recognised at Rome.
The date historians normally use falls in the 20s BCE.

acceptedIdeas: the senate granted octavian the name augustus in 27 bce
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus in 27 BCE.

choices.label: Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE
The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus in 27 BCE
Rome was founded, by tradition, in 753 BCE
The last western emperor was deposed in 476 CE

questions.prompt: By the traditional date, in which year BCE did the Roman Republic begin? Give the year as a number with the era.
hints: The Republic began when Rome expelled its last king.
The traditional date falls in the sixth century BCE.
Give the year as a number followed by the era, for example 400 BCE.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rome expelled its last king in 509 BCE by the traditional dating, and the Republic ran from that year.

questions.prompt: Explain one thing that stayed the same and one thing that changed when Augustus took power in 27 BCE.
hints: Think about which republican institutions a Roman of the day could still see working.
Then think about who actually decided the army and the provinces after 27 BCE.
Name one continuity and one change in your answer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The republican offices continued to be filled and elections still took place, so the outward form of the Republic stayed in place. What changed was that one man held the powers over the army and the provinces, so decisions no longer rested with the Senate.

questions.prompt: Describe what made the Republic's system of shared, temporary power break down in the first century BCE.
hints: Consider how long some commanders held their provincial commands.
Ask who the soldiers in those armies felt they owed loyalty to.
Connect that loyalty to what happened in 49 BCE.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Commanders held long provincial commands and their soldiers became loyal to them rather than to the state. That made civil war possible, and Caesar's march into Italy in 49 BCE began one.

questions.prompt: What was a Roman provincial governor answerable to Rome for?
hints: A governor's job combined military command with civil authority.
One duty in particular was measured and reported back to Rome.
Think about what the imperial treasury expected from a province.

acceptedIdeas: the order of his province and the taxes it produced
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The order of his province and the taxes it produced.

choices.label: The order of his province and the taxes it produced
Electing the magistrates who served in Rome
Choosing the next emperor when a reign ended
Writing the law code used across the empire

questions.prompt: In which year CE did the Roman Empire reach its greatest territorial extent? Give the year as a number with the era.
hints: The greatest extent came at the death of one emperor, Trajan.
The year falls early in the second century CE.
Give the year as a number followed by the era, for example 200 CE.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The empire covered its largest area in 117 CE, at the death of Trajan.

questions.prompt: Explain how the road network helped Rome keep control of provinces that were far from the city.
hints: Start with what the roads were originally built for.
Think about what a paved, graded surface does to travel time in bad weather.
Connect predictable travel time to how orders and reports moved.

rejectedIdeas: roads were built mainly for trade
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The roads were built for the army, with a paved and graded surface that stayed usable in winter. That made travel time predictable, so troops could be moved and a governor's report could reach Rome on a known schedule.

questions.prompt: How did Rome usually administer a newly annexed province with only a few thousand officials?
hints: Rome did not replace every local office-holder after a conquest.
Consider who already knew how to collect a local tax.
Pick the option that describes working through people already in place.

acceptedIdeas: by leaving local elites in place to collect much of what rome asked for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By leaving local elites in place to collect much of what Rome asked for.

choices.label: By replacing every local official with a Roman citizen from Italy
By leaving local elites in place to collect much of what Rome asked for
By granting each province full independence in exchange for tribute
By stationing the whole Roman army inside the new province

questions.prompt: In which year CE was the last emperor in the west deposed? Give the year as a number with the era.
hints: The emperor deposed was Romulus Augustulus.
The year falls in the second half of the fifth century CE.
Give the year as a number followed by the era, for example 400 CE.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE and no successor was appointed in the west.

questions.prompt: What happened to the Roman state in the east after 476 CE?
hints: Locate 476 CE on the timeline.
Recall which capital governed the continuing eastern rule.

acceptedIdeas: Rule continued in the east, governed from Constantinople.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rule continued in the east, governed from Constantinople.

choices.label: Rule continued in the east, governed from Constantinople.
The entire Roman Empire ended immediately.
A new western emperor was appointed.
Constantinople was abandoned as a capital.

questions.prompt: What did the Antonine Constitution of 212 CE change?
hints: Recall who received a new legal status.
State how widely the change applied.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It extended Roman citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the empire, placing them under the same body of law.

questions.prompt: Name two things Roman rule left behind in western Europe and say why each lasted.
hints: Choose two legacies named in the lesson.
One concerns the language people went on speaking.
For each, say what kept it in use once the state was gone.

rejectedIdeas: nothing roman survived in the west
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Roman law lasted because later rulers kept applying its rules, and Latin lasted because the languages descended from it stayed in everyday speech. The road lines also stayed in use, because the routes still went where people needed to travel.

questions.prompt: Who paid for the public buildings of a Roman city, and what did they expect in return?
hints: Identify the two groups who funded the buildings.
Recall the social benefit donors expected.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Emperors and wealthy citizens paid for them, and they expected public recognition in return.

flashcards.front: By tradition, in which year did the Roman Republic begin and what happened in that year?
flashcards.back: 509 BCE, when Rome expelled its last king and began electing magistrates for fixed terms.

flashcards.front: Which event is normally taken as the start of rule by an emperor at Rome?
flashcards.back: The settlement of 27 BCE, when the Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus.

flashcards.front: What was decided at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE?
flashcards.back: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, which left him without a rival for control of the Roman world.

flashcards.front: When did the Roman Empire cover its largest area?
flashcards.back: In 117 CE, at the death of Trajan, when it reached from Britain to Mesopotamia.

flashcards.front: What were Roman paved roads built for?
flashcards.back: For the army. A graded paved surface kept travel time predictable, which also carried official messengers and trade.

flashcards.front: What happened to Roman rule in the west in 476 CE?
flashcards.back: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and no new emperor was appointed in the west.

flashcards.front: What did the Antonine Constitution of 212 CE do?
flashcards.back: It extended Roman citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the empire.

flashcards.front: What continued in the east after the western empire’s end in 476 CE?
flashcards.back: Rule continued from Constantinople for nearly another thousand years.

essays.title: Roads and administration
essays.prompt: Explain how roads and provincial administration together allowed Rome to govern territory that was weeks of travel away from the city. Use at least one date or example from the lesson.
essays.expectedScope: A short argument of four to eight sentences that connects the physical network to the administrative one.
successCriteria: Explains what the road network did to the time and reliability of travel.
Describes the governor's role and what he answered to Rome for.
Explains why leaving local elites in place made a small administration workable.
Uses at least one date or named example accurately.

essays.title: What outlasted Roman rule
essays.prompt: The last western emperor was deposed in 476 CE. Explain what parts of Roman rule outlasted that date, and why each of them survived the state that created it.
essays.expectedScope: A short argument of four to eight sentences covering at least two distinct legacies.
successCriteria: States accurately what did and did not end in 476 CE.
Identifies at least two things that outlasted western imperial rule.
Gives a reason each one survived rather than listing them alone.
